# DATASET A — Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields (1990–2025)

*Wide file for Sections 1–3; long file for Section 4.*

## Section 1 — Descriptive Statistics

### A-1-1
Filter to `Year = 2023` and work with the **Canola** column.

**(a)** Compute the mean and median canola yield.
**(b)** The mean (≈33.9) comes out *below* the median (≈35.5). In one or two sentences, explain what that gap tells you about how yields were distributed across RMs that year — in particular, what it implies about the low-yielding RMs.
**(c)** A classmate reports the mean as 33.9 and concludes "so a typical RM grew about 34 bu/ac." Do you agree that the mean is the best summary of a *typical* RM here? Justify your answer using the mean-vs-median comparison.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) mean ≈ 33.88, median ≈ 35.50 bu/ac.
- (b) Mean below median signals a **left/low tail** — a minority of RMs with unusually *low* yields (down to ~3 bu/ac) drag the mean beneath the median. Most RMs cluster higher; a few poor ones pull the average down.
- (c) The **median (≈35.5) is the more honest "typical" value**; the mean is depressed by the low-yield tail. Full credit for naming the median as more representative *and* tying it to the skew.
</details>

### A-1-2
Still on 2023, compare **Canola** and **Barley**.

**(a)** Compute the standard deviation of each. Barley's SD (≈24.6) is much larger than canola's (≈13.3). Does that alone prove barley yields are "more variable" in a meaningful sense? Explain the trap.
**(b)** Compute the **coefficient of variation (CV)** for each and use it to make a fair comparison of *relative* variability.
**(c)** Write one sentence a farm reporter could publish, correctly stating which crop's yields were more variable relative to their average.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) No — barley also has a much higher *mean* (≈54.6 vs ≈33.9), so a bigger SD is partly just scale. Comparing raw SDs across crops with different means is the trap.
- (b) CV = SD/mean. Canola ≈ 13.3/33.9 ≈ **0.39**; Barley ≈ 24.6/54.6 ≈ **0.45**. Barley is *slightly* more variable relative to its mean.
- (c) e.g. "Relative to their average yields, Saskatchewan barley yields in 2023 were a bit more variable than canola (CV 0.45 vs 0.39)."
</details>

## Section 2 — Conditional Functions & Lookups

### A-2-1
Use the full (all-years) dataset.

**(a)** Use `AVERAGEIF` to find the average canola yield in **2010**, **2021**, and **2023**.
**(b)** 2021 (≈21.9) sits far below 2010 (≈29.8) and 2023 (≈33.9). Which single word best describes 2021 in Saskatchewan agriculture, and what feature of the data would you point to as evidence?
**(c)** Your `AVERAGEIF` for 2023 returns a number even though six RMs have a **blank** canola cell that year. Explain what `AVERAGEIF` did with those blanks, and why filling them with 0 would have been wrong.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) 2010 ≈ 29.82, 2021 ≈ 21.86, 2023 ≈ 33.88 bu/ac. `=AVERAGEIF(A:A, 2021, E:E)`.
- (b) **Drought.** Evidence: every crop's average (not just canola) drops in 2021 — a broad, year-wide fall rather than one crop.
- (c) `AVERAGEIF` **skips blank cells**, averaging only the RMs that reported. Filling blanks with 0 would count "no data" as "a yield of zero," dragging the average down artificially.
</details>

### A-2-2
**(a)** Use `COUNTIF` to count how many RM-year rows have canola yield **above 40 bu/ac** across all years.
**(b)** Use a two-criteria lookup (`XLOOKUP` on a combined RM+Year key, or `INDEX`/`MATCH`) to pull the canola yield for **RM 1 in 2023**.
**(c)** Suppose you instead used a plain `VLOOKUP` on RM number alone to get "RM 1's canola yield." Explain why that would return a misleading answer for a dataset that spans 1990–2025.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) ≈ 1483 rows. `=COUNTIF(E:E, ">40")`.
- (b) ≈ 36.8 bu/ac. `=XLOOKUP(1&"|"&2023, B:B&"|"&A:A, E:E)`.
- (c) RM 1 appears in ~36 different years; `VLOOKUP` on RM alone returns the **first match only** (one arbitrary year), not the 2023 value. You must match on RM *and* Year.
</details>

## Section 3 — Charts

### A-3-1
Filter to `Year = 2023`, Canola column.

**(a)** Build a histogram of 2023 canola yields (≈10–15 bins), with a descriptive title and labelled axes.
**(b)** Describe the **shape** in Module-1 terms (symmetric? skewed? which direction?), and point to the specific feature of the histogram that supports your description.
**(c)** Would you summarize the centre of *this* histogram with the mean or the median? Tie your choice to the shape you described in (b).

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Histogram; title e.g. "Distribution of Canola Yields Across Saskatchewan RMs, 2023", x = "Yield (bu/ac)", y = "Number of RMs".
- (b) **Left/low-skewed** — the bulk sits in the 30s–40s with a longer thin tail stretching toward the low single digits.
- (c) The **median**, because the low tail pulls the mean below the typical value. (Grading: 20% of this section's marks are the chart's visual quality — title, axis labels, sensible bins.)
</details>

### A-3-2
**(a)** Build a single box-and-whisker chart comparing **Canola, Spring Wheat, and Barley** yields in 2023 (three boxes).
**(b)** Which crop shows the widest box, and what does box *width* represent? State what that means about that crop's yields in plain language.
**(c)** A reader asks "which crop is most reliable to grow?" Explain what the box plot can and cannot tell them about that — staying within what this chart actually shows.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Box-and-whisker, three crops; titled, axes labelled.
- (b) **Barley** has the widest box (IQR ≈ 41 vs canola ≈ 22). Box width = the **interquartile range**, the spread of the middle 50% of RMs — so barley yields varied most across RMs.
- (c) It shows spread and centre (a wider/lower box = less consistent yields), which speaks to *variability*. It does **not** show profitability, price, or cost, so "most reliable to grow" can only be answered on the yield-consistency part. (No probability/likelihood language — not yet introduced.)
</details>

## Section 4 — PivotTables

*Use the **long** file (`rm_yields_1990plus_long.csv`).*

### A-4-1
**(a)** Build a PivotTable of **average yield by crop for 2023** (Year in Filters = 2023, Crop on Rows, Yield as Average). Rank the crops.
**(b)** Lentils appear at ≈1314 while the next crop is ≈71. Explain why — and what a reader would wrongly conclude if they took the ranking at face value.
**(c)** Add `Unit` to Filters and set it to `bu/ac`. Now which crop is highest and which lowest, and why is this the *fair* comparison?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Lentils ≈1314 (lb/ac), Oats ≈71, Barley ≈55, Spring Wheat ≈43, Peas ≈34, Canola ≈34, Durum ≈30, Flax ≈20 (bu/ac).
- (b) Lentils are in **lb/ac**, everything else bu/ac. Taken at face value a reader would think lentils out-yield oats ~18×, which is a **unit artifact**, not agronomy.
- (c) Filtered to bu/ac: **Oats highest (≈71), Flax lowest (≈20).** Fair because all crops share one unit.
</details>

### A-4-2
**(a)** Build a PivotTable with Year on Rows and Crop on Columns (Yield as Average, Unit filtered to bu/ac). Read down the columns.
**(b)** Compare canola in **2021 (≈21.9)** vs **2023 (≈33.9)**. Describe the size of the gap in plain language.
**(c)** 2021 is low for *every* crop, not just canola. Explain how the crop-by-year grid lets you distinguish a **whole-year shock** (like drought) from a problem affecting only one crop.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Year × Crop grid of average yields.
- (b) 2021 canola is about **one-third lower** than 2023 (≈12 bu/ac less) — a large drop.
- (c) If a *whole row* (year) is low across all crop columns, the cause is broad (weather/drought). If a single *column* (crop) dips in one year while others hold, the cause is crop-specific (a pest/disease). The grid shows rows vs columns at a glance.
</details>

# DATASET B — Manitoba Red Spring Wheat by Variety (2020–2025)

*Single file `mb_wheat_varieties.csv`; `Reported` = TRUE/FALSE (FALSE = MASC suppressed the yield because too few farms grew it).*

## Section 1 — Descriptive Statistics

### B-1-1
Work with the **reported** yields only (`Reported = TRUE`, i.e. non-blank `Yield_bu_ac`).

**(a)** Compute the mean, median, and IQR of reported yields.
**(b)** Mean ≈61.2 and median ≈62.2 are very close. What does that near-equality suggest about the shape, compared with the skewed Saskatchewan canola data?
**(c)** The CV here is ≈0.20, versus ≈0.39 for SK 2023 canola. Interpret that contrast in one sentence a grower would understand.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) mean ≈61.16, median ≈62.20, IQR ≈15.7 bu/ac.
- (b) Mean ≈ median → **roughly symmetric**, unlike the left-skewed SK canola. Variety trials on established ground give tighter, more centred yields.
- (c) e.g. "Relative to their average, these wheat yields vary about half as much as Saskatchewan canola did in 2023 (CV 0.20 vs 0.39) — a more consistent crop-and-place."
</details>

### B-1-2
**(a)** Compute the 90th percentile of reported yields and state, in plain language, what it means.
**(b)** Compute the minimum reported yield. It is far below the rest. Before calling it an error, give one *real* agronomic reason a genuine 4–5 bu/ac wheat yield could occur.
**(c)** Explain why the median barely moves if that one low value is removed, but the mean would shift more — using what you know about how each responds to extreme values.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) P90 ≈ 75.8 bu/ac — 90% of reported variety-municipality results were at or below this; only the top 10% exceeded it.
- (b) A localized drought/hail/flood or a failed field can genuinely yield a handful of bushels — low, but real, not necessarily a typo.
- (c) The **median** is a position (the middle value) and ignores how far away extremes are, so one low point barely moves it; the **mean** sums every value, so an extreme low pulls it down. This is the module's mean-vs-outlier point.
</details>

## Section 2 — Conditional Functions & Lookups

### B-2-1
**(a)** Use `COUNTIF`/`COUNTIFS` to count how many rows are **suppressed** (`Reported = FALSE`) vs reported (TRUE).
**(b)** Suppressed rows outnumber reported ones (≈2960 vs ≈2398). Explain what a suppressed row *means* here, and why it is a **different kind of "missing"** than a blank in the Saskatchewan file.
**(c)** A student deletes all suppressed rows before analysing. Give one situation where that is fine and one where it would bias a conclusion.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) ≈2960 FALSE, ≈2398 TRUE. `=COUNTIF(G:G, "FALSE")`.
- (b) Suppressed = the variety *was* grown in that municipality but too few farms reported for MASC to publish a number (privacy). Different from the SK blanks, which mean the crop **wasn't grown** at all.
- (c) Fine: computing the average yield *among reported results*. Biased: claiming "variety X is rarely grown" from few reported rows — it may be widely grown but suppressed. Absence of a number ≠ absence of the crop.
</details>

### B-2-2
**(a)** Use `AVERAGEIF` to compute the average reported yield for the variety **AAC BRANDON (BW 932)**.
**(b)** Use a lookup to find AAC Brandon's yield in a specific municipality-year of your choice, then say why a single such number is a weak basis for choosing a variety.
**(c)** Explain why comparing two varieties fairly requires accounting for *how many* municipalities reported each (hint: `COUNTIF` on the variety), not just their average yields.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) ≈ 59.6 bu/ac (most-grown variety, n≈519 reported).
- (b) A single municipality-year reflects that place's weather/soil that year; variety choice should rest on the average across many sites/years, not one point.
- (c) An average over 5 reports is far less trustworthy than one over 500; a variety can look "best" off a handful of lucky sites. Report counts show how much weight each average deserves.
</details>

## Section 3 — Charts

### B-3-1
**(a)** Build a histogram of all reported wheat yields, titled with labelled axes.
**(b)** Describe the shape and contrast it with the Saskatchewan canola histogram from Dataset A.
**(c)** By the 1.5×IQR rule, this data has genuine low-end outliers (≈39 of them). Explain how a box plot would display them and why a histogram alone might not make you call them "outliers".

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Histogram, titled/labelled.
- (b) **Roughly symmetric and tighter** (bulk 54–70) vs the left-skewed, wider SK canola — reflecting controlled variety trials.
- (c) A box plot marks points beyond Q1−1.5·IQR (here below ≈30) as **individual dots past the whisker**, flagging them explicitly; a histogram just shows a low tail, leaving "outlier" a judgment call. This is the module's box-plot outlier convention.
</details>

### B-3-2
**(a)** Pick the six most-reported varieties and build a box plot comparing their yield distributions (one box each).
**(b)** Explain what a reader learns from the box plot that a simple bar chart of *average* yield per variety would hide.
**(c)** You want to show a non-technical audience "these top varieties yield similarly." Would you choose the box plot or a bar chart of means, and why? (Answer in terms of audience and message, per the module's chart-choice guidance.)

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Box plot, up to six varieties, titled/labelled.
- (b) The box plot shows **spread and consistency** (some varieties more variable than others) and flags outliers — a bar of means shows only the centre and hides all of that.
- (c) Defensible either way *if justified*: bar-of-means is cleaner for a lay audience whose takeaway is "similar averages"; the box plot is right if the point is consistency. Credit the reasoning about audience + message, not the specific pick.
</details>

## Section 4 — PivotTables

### B-4-1
**(a)** Build a PivotTable of **average reported yield by variety** (Variety on Rows, Yield_bu_ac as Average). Add a Count to see how many reports back each average.
**(b)** The top variety by average (**SY MANNESS**, ≈72) beats the most-*grown* variety (**AAC Brandon**, ≈60). Explain why "highest average" and "most widely grown" can differ, and which you'd trust more for a planting decision.
**(c)** Explain why filtering the PivotTable to varieties with a minimum number of reports (say ≥30) gives a more trustworthy ranking than including every variety.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Variety on Rows; Yield as Average + Count.
- (b) A niche variety on a few good sites can post a high average without being widely adopted; AAC Brandon's ≈60 rests on ~519 reports. Trust the widely-reported average as a decision base; a high average on thin data is fragile.
- (c) Averages from 1–2 reports are noisy and can top the list by luck; a ≥30 threshold keeps only well-supported estimates, making the ranking meaningful.
</details>

### B-4-2
**(a)** Build a PivotTable with Variety on Rows and Year on Columns (Yield as Average) for AAC Brandon and a few common varieties.
**(b)** AAC Brandon dips in **2021 (≈49)** versus ≈62–66 in other years. Given what you saw in the Saskatchewan data, what most likely caused the 2021 dip across Manitoba varieties too?
**(c)** Explain how looking at the *same variety across years* separates a variety's genetic potential from year-to-year weather effects.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Variety × Year grid.
- (b) The **2021 drought** hit Manitoba as well — the dip appears across varieties in that year, i.e. a weather effect, not a variety fault. (Nice cross-dataset consistency with the SK 2021 drop.)
- (c) Holding the variety fixed and reading across years isolates weather (all years share the same genetics), while comparing varieties within a year isolates genetics (all share the same weather).
</details>

# DATASET C — Canada Field Crops by Province (StatsCan, 2015–2025)

*Single file `statcan_field_crops.csv`: columns Year, Province, Crop, Seeded_acres, Yield_bu_ac.*

## Section 1 — Descriptive Statistics

### C-1-1
Filter to **Spring wheat** (all provinces, all years).

**(a)** Compute mean, median, and range of spring wheat yield.
**(b)** The range is large because provinces differ hugely (a maritime province vs the Prairies). Explain why a single national mean can be a *misleading* summary when the data pools very different provinces.
**(c)** Suggest a better way to summarize "spring wheat yield in Canada" than one overall mean, using only Module-1 tools.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) mean ≈ 51.3, median ≈ 50.8, range ≈ 33.7 to 73.9 bu/ac.
- (b) Pooling provinces with very different yields hides real structure — the "national average" describes no actual province well.
- (c) Break it out **by province** (a PivotTable or AVERAGEIF per province), and/or show a box plot per province — summarize the groups, not just the pool.
</details>

### C-1-2
Filter to **Canola** (all provinces, all years).

**(a)** Compute the CV of canola yield and compare it to the CV of spring wheat from C-1-1.
**(b)** Interpret which crop's provincial yields are more consistent across the country, in one plain sentence.
**(c)** A colleague computed a canola yield of "0 bu/ac" for one province-year in the raw StatsCan table. Explain why treating that 0 as a real yield would distort the mean, and what it more likely represented.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Canola CV ≈ 0.13 vs spring wheat CV ≈ 0.15 (both computed SD/mean).
- (b) e.g. "Across provinces and years, canola yields were slightly more consistent than spring wheat, relative to their averages."
- (c) A real 0 would pull the mean down and isn't meaningful (no crop truly yields 0 on 0 acres); it was a **placeholder/negligible-acreage code**, correctly treated as missing (why the cleaned file drops it).
</details>

## Section 2 — Conditional Functions & Lookups

### C-2-1
**(a)** Use `SUMIF` to compute the **total canola seeded acres across all provinces in 2023**.
**(b)** The total is ≈22.1 million acres. Using `SUMIF` per province (or a quick sort), name which province dominates that total and what that implies about where the "national" canola number really comes from.
**(c)** Explain why summing `Seeded_acres` is valid but summing `Yield_bu_ac` across provinces would be meaningless.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) ≈ 22,085,300 acres. `=SUMIF` on Crop=Canola, Year=2023.
- (b) **Saskatchewan** dominates (largest seeded area), so national canola figures are largely a Saskatchewan story.
- (c) Acres are an **extensive** quantity — they add up. Yield (bu *per acre*) is a **rate/intensity**; adding rates across provinces has no meaning (you'd average them, ideally weighted by acres).
</details>

### C-2-2
**(a)** Use `COUNTIF`/`COUNTIFS` to count how many province-crop-year rows have a **blank** yield.
**(b)** Blanks concentrate in certain crop-province pairs (e.g. flax or durum in eastern provinces). Explain what a blank means here and why it is *expected*, not an error.
**(c)** A lookup for "durum yield in Nova Scotia, 2022" returns blank. Explain, in one sentence, the correct way to report that result rather than writing 0 or "error".

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) ≈ 185 rows blank (as of snapshot). `=COUNTBLANK` or `COUNTIF` on the yield column.
- (b) Blank = that crop **isn't meaningfully grown** in that province/year, so StatsCan publishes no yield — expected geography, not a data fault.
- (c) Report it as "not grown / not reported" (leave blank), never 0 — 0 would falsely imply a real measured zero yield.
</details>

## Section 3 — Charts

### C-3-1
**(a)** Build a box plot comparing **canola yield across provinces** (one box per province) using all years 2015–2025.
**(b)** Which provinces sit highest, and which show the most spread? Say what "spread" means for a province here.
**(c)** A headline claims "Ontario grows the best canola." Explain what your box plot supports and what it does **not** (e.g., scale of production), staying within the chart.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Box plot, province on the category axis.
- (b) **Ontario** highest average (~47), Prairie provinces mid; spread = the range/IQR of a province's year-to-year yields — wider box = more variable across years.
- (c) The box plot supports "higher *yield per acre* in Ontario," but says nothing about **how much** canola each province grows (acreage) — Saskatchewan produces vastly more despite lower per-acre yield. Yield ≠ production.
</details>

### C-3-2
**(a)** Using a PivotTable feeding a chart, make a **line chart of average Canadian canola yield by year** (2015–2025).
**(b)** Identify the lowest year on the chart and connect it to what you have seen in the other two datasets.
**(c)** Would a line chart or a pie chart be the right tool to show this "yield over time" story? Justify using the module's chart-choice guidance.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Line chart, year on x, average yield on y, titled/labelled.
- (b) **2021** is the low point — the same drought that hit the SK RM data and Manitoba varieties. Cross-dataset consistency.
- (c) **Line chart** — it shows change over an ordered variable (time). A pie chart shows parts of a whole at one moment and cannot show a trend; the module explicitly cautions against pie charts here.
</details>

## Section 4 — PivotTables

### C-4-1
**(a)** Build a PivotTable of **average canola yield by province for 2023** (Province on Rows, Yield as Average, Year filtered to 2023).
**(b)** Rank the provinces. Ontario (~53) tops Saskatchewan (~37). Does that mean Ontario is the more important canola province? Explain what this pivot does and does not establish.
**(c)** Add `Seeded_acres` as a second value (Sum). Explain how looking at yield *and* acreage together changes the story from yield alone.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Province on Rows, Yield Average, Year=2023.
- (b) Ranking is by **yield per acre**, on which Ontario leads. It does **not** establish importance/output — Saskatchewan's far larger acreage means it produces much more canola overall.
- (c) Yield shows per-acre performance; acreage shows scale. Together: Ontario yields more per acre but SK dominates total production. The two columns tell a fuller story than either alone.
</details>

### C-4-2
**(a)** Build a PivotTable with Province on Rows and Year on Columns (canola Yield as Average).
**(b)** Reading across Saskatchewan's row, identify its weakest year and state the gap to a normal year in plain language.
**(c)** Explain how this province × year grid lets you tell whether 2021 was a *local* Saskatchewan problem or a *national* one — and what you conclude.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Province × Year grid of average canola yield.
- (b) Saskatchewan's **2021** is well below its other years — a substantial drop (SK canola ~22 vs ~37 in 2023 in the RM data; the provincial StatsCan figure shows the same direction).
- (c) If 2021 is low **down the whole column** (most provinces), it's a broad/national drought year; if only SK's cell is low, it's local. Reading the column shows multiple Prairie provinces down together → widespread drought.
</details>

## Notes for review

- **Every question has a compute part AND an interpret/communicate part** — the interpretation is the point, calculation is the setup.
- **Vocabulary stays inside Module 1**: symmetric/skewed, mean-vs-median, range/IQR/SD/CV, percentiles, box-plot whiskers & 1.5×IQR outliers, histogram shape, pie-vs-bar/line chart choice, wide/long, pivot grouping, yield-vs-production, rate-vs-total. **No** normality, correlation, probability, sampling, significance.
- **Cross-dataset thread**: the 2021 drought recurs in all three, so students who do multiple quizzes see the same real event three ways.
- **Chart & pivot sections lean hardest on presentation and reading**, matching the 20%-visual weighting.
- Section 4 answers assume the SK **long** file; Datasets B and C are already long-shaped.
